title: Engineering a better text-to-CAD brief
summary: Turn a flange description into dimensions, geometric checks and an export you can inspect.
content_html:
A useful text-to-CAD brief describes a part and defines how to tell whether the result is correct. A polished render can make an incorrect hole pattern look convincing. Dimensions, coordinate conventions and acceptance checks make the request inspectable. Intact combines a conversational assistant with local geometry tools, so the brief should give both something precise to work with.

Start with a complete, bounded example

Consider this request: “Create an 80 mm diameter pipe flange, 8 mm thick, with a 24 mm bore and six 6 mm through holes on a 60 mm bolt circle. Keep the bore concentric with the outside diameter. Verify the hole positions and export STEP.” It specifies a single part, a repeating feature and a useful deliverable. It also leaves fewer opportunities to confuse a radius with a diameter.

The bundled flange example constructs a cylinder, subtracts a central bore and places six cutters at 60-degree intervals. Its parameter catalog records an expected 80 × 80 × 8 mm bounding box and one output part. These are useful starting checks, rather than a complete manufacturing specification.

Separate dimensions from assumptions

Write “bolt circle diameter 60 mm,” or “60 mm PCD,” rather than “holes at 60 mm.” The hole centers belong on a radius of 30 mm. State that the holes pass through the entire 8 mm thickness. Specify the reference plane and angular orientation if the flange must align with another part. For an isolated demonstration, the first hole can lie on positive X and the pattern can proceed around the Z axis.

With that convention, the nominal XY centers are (30, 0), (15, 25.981), (−15, 25.981), (−30, 0), (−15, −25.981) and (15, −25.981) mm. The rounded coordinates are explanatory; the construction uses trigonometric positions. An inspection should compare measured centers against the intended circle and angular spacing using an explicitly chosen tolerance.

Add only the details the job needs

A flange for a visual layout may need only nominal geometry. A flange for a physical interface also needs material, mating dimensions, tolerances and any required edge treatment. Do not let an assistant invent a seal groove, countersink or thread because those features are common elsewhere. Ask for clarification when a missing dimension changes fit or function.

Make verification part of the request

Ask for native validity, one solid, overall dimensions, bore diameter and the six-hole pattern. Hole count alone is insufficient: six holes on the wrong circle still satisfy it. Check diameter, through state, center positions and axis direction together. Intact can save structured requirements and check actual exported geometry; a feature named “6 mm hole” is not evidence that the final hole measures 6 mm.

Choose tolerance deliberately. A computational comparison tolerance expresses how closely a measurement must match the requested nominal value. It does not establish a machining process capability, a physical inspection result or a fit class. Likewise, a kernel tolerance is numerical metadata. Keep those distinctions visible when sharing a verification report.

Preserve intent when making revisions

A follow-up should identify what changes and what must survive: “Increase the flange thickness to 10 mm. Preserve the 80 mm outside diameter, 24 mm bore and six-hole pattern. Update the thickness requirement and verify the STEP again.” Updating the requirement matters: a deliberate design change should not remain in conflict with the old acceptance target.

For structured projects, parameters, solved sketches and supported feature operations can retain editable intent. Arbitrary imported STEP does not automatically acquire a recovered parametric history. Establish which workflow the current model uses before promising a parameter edit.

Choose an export for its next use

STEP is appropriate when the recipient needs the native solid representation. STL, GLB and 3MF serve different mesh and presentation workflows. Verify the actual exported file and record its units alongside the dimensions. Geometry validity and nominal checks do not certify pressure service, fatigue life or manufacturing readiness.

Explore the prebuilt browser demo to see the interaction, then use the desktop setup for real CAD execution. The workflow guide explains how the assistant, local tools and viewer fit together.

title: A reproducible 1000 N compression benchmark
summary: Use a simple block to check structural load signs, units, reactions and mesh refinement.
content_html:
A small compression block is a useful place to test a structural workflow because its expected response can be calculated independently. The point is to compare a numerical result with a known solution, then inspect the evidence behind that result. A colored deformation plot by itself cannot establish that the load, material and supports mean what the user intended.

Define the problem before solving it

The Intact 0.16 verification case uses one native solid measuring 10 × 10 × 20 mm. Its cross-sectional area is 100 mm² and its height is 20 mm. The material has Young’s modulus E = 10 GPa and Poisson’s ratio ν = 0. Fix the bottom face and apply a total downward force of 1000 N to the top face, along native CAD −Z.

“Total force” is important. It is not 1000 N per node and not a pressure of 1000 in an unspecified unit system. The fixed bottom prevents displacement there; the load acts on the opposing top face. Record the actual face selections so an apparently correct setup cannot conceal a force applied to the wrong surface.

Compute the reference answer

For uniform axial compression, displacement magnitude is u = FL/(EA). Convert the modulus to compatible units: 10 GPa = 10,000 N/mm². Substitution gives 1000 × 20 / (10,000 × 100) = 0.020 mm. The loaded top moves in negative Z; 0.020 mm is the magnitude of its compression displacement.

The axial stress magnitude is F/A = 1000/100 = 10 N/mm², or 10 MPa. With a uniaxial stress state, the von Mises equivalent stress has the same magnitude. The fixed support should supply a positive Z reaction of 1000 N to balance the negative Z load. Poisson’s ratio zero removes lateral contraction coupling from this simple reference case.

Compare with actual solver evidence

The 0.16 release verification reports a live local AI-to-solver-to-viewer run with displacement 0.020000000000000122 mm, peak element-average von Mises stress 10 MPa and Z reaction 999.9999999999994 N. The final mesh had 208 nodes and 588 tetrahedra. Those small differences from the hand calculation are consistent with numerical arithmetic.

The same report records a residual of approximately 1.02 × 10⁻¹⁴ and a force-balance error of approximately 6.47 × 10⁻¹⁶. These are reported numerical diagnostics, not physical uncertainties or manufacturing tolerances. Read their definitions in the solver context before comparing values from another solver or another problem.

Refinement is part of the check

A single mesh can agree accidentally, particularly on a simple geometry. The reported benchmark passed displacement and stress refinement checks. When reproducing it, retain mesh counts, quality information, convergence status and results at successive resolutions. Look for stable quantities within the chosen acceptance target rather than merely selecting the smallest element size available.

Resource limits also matter. A refinement that stops at a budget without meeting its target should remain unverified. A failed or nonconverged run needs review; preparing a study or displaying an answer is not equivalent to completing a successful numerical analysis.

A practical reproduction brief

Ask the desktop workflow to create or inspect the block, confirm millimeter dimensions, select the bottom support and top load, and report the stated material properties. Then request the actual static structural solution, displacement direction and magnitude, stress, summed reaction, residual, mesh information and refinement evidence. Preserve the native geometry and revision during the study.

Keep the analytical calculation beside the result. If displacement differs by a factor of 1000, investigate unit conversion before interpreting a plot. If the reaction has the wrong sign or magnitude, inspect axes, support selection and load interpretation. These simple checks are often more informative than adding visual detail.

Know what the benchmark establishes

This is a single-solid compression test. It does not predict the bending of a vehicle, validate an entire assembly or exercise contact between parts. Intact’s supported structural scope does not include whole-assembly contact, nonlinear mechanics or production certification. A separate softer 1 GPa case reached the small-strain acceptance boundary and correctly required review.

The browser demo illustrates a prebuilt interaction; it does not execute this solver. Follow local setup for native Windows x86-64 computation and read how the workflow operates before interpreting results.

title: TPMS: from an implicit equation to a sampled gyroid
summary: Understand the difference between an implicit surface, a triangle mesh and a native CAD solid.
content_html:
A gyroid can look like a smoothly flowing solid in a viewer, but its representation matters as much as its appearance. An implicit equation describes a field. Sampling turns that field into finite data. A mesh extraction turns those samples into triangles. None of those steps automatically produces an exact smooth boundary representation suitable for native STEP editing.

Begin with the field

Intact’s gyroid field uses F = sin(x)cos(y) + sin(y)cos(z) + sin(z)cos(x), with coordinates scaled by the requested cell size. A level selects a field value. In sheet mode, the basic construction retains a band around that level. At zero gradient, its condition is |F − level| ≤ band. This is a nodal TPMS approximation, rather than a claim to an exact minimal surface.

The bundled gyroid example requests a 24 × 24 × 24 mm envelope, 8 mm cell size, band 0.3 and 16 samples per cell. That spans three nominal cells along each direction. Those settings are recorded in the example catalog, making the starting geometry reproducible.

A band is not a wall thickness

The basic band parameter is dimensionless. It measures a range of field values, not a distance in millimeters. Because the field gradient varies spatially, a fixed field band does not imply constant physical wall thickness. Calling band 0.3 a “0.3 mm wall” changes the meaning of the model and can mislead a printability or strength assessment.

Intact also has distance-offset workflows with separate millimeter controls. Use those controls when requesting a distance-based thickness and inspect the resulting sampling and validation limits. A millimeter input alone does not remove approximation error. If minimum thickness is a requirement, ask how it was measured and what portions of the surface were checked.

Sampling determines the delivered geometry

The implementation samples the field on a bounded grid, clips it to an envelope and uses marching cubes to extract a triangle surface. For the basic 24 mm, 8 mm cell, 16-sample example, nominal grid spacing is 0.5 mm per axis before boundary padding. A smooth shaded render can hide this finite sampling.

The lattice helper caps the clipped result and checks for a positive, closed volume with consistent winding. It also records sampling spacing, estimated mesh volume and relative density. These checks are valuable, but they do not establish an exact smooth geometry or a globally certified minimum wall thickness.

Refine with a purpose

Keep envelope, cell size, phase and band fixed while increasing resolution. Compare sampled volume and surface area and inspect thin connections and envelope boundaries. A large change indicates that the coarser mesh was not a stable description of the quantity you need. Increasing resolution also increases memory and triangle counts, so bounded sampling budgets remain part of the workflow.

Six families, explicit choices

The available sampled families are gyroid, Schwarz P, diamond, neovius, lidinoid and split P. Changing a family changes the field; it is not merely a display style. Record the family name alongside cell size, mode, level, band, phase, envelope and sampling resolution so another person can reconstruct the same request.

Sheet mode retains material around a field level. Solid mode retains one side of that level. Those choices can produce very different material fractions and connectivity. Select the mode explicitly before comparing density or making mechanical interpretations. Similar-looking lattices do not necessarily have equivalent stiffness or manufacturability.

Choose an honest export

The bundled gyroid lists STL, GLB and 3MF outputs. These carry mesh geometry. Native solid parts elsewhere in Intact can use STEP, but an implicit lattice mesh does not gain exact smooth CAD surfaces just because STEP is requested. A separate faceted conversion is available within limits; its faces still describe a faceted approximation.

The optional PicoGK path provides voxel-based TPMS workflows. It is an additional local dependency and returns mesh geometry, not smooth STEP. Choose it for its supported voxel operations, rather than as a promise to recover an analytic CAD surface.

Connect representation to the next decision

For visualization, a sampled mesh may be sufficient. For printing, inspect mesh integrity, resolution, physical thickness and process constraints. For analysis, document how the lattice is represented and whether the chosen solver actually supports that geometry. A lattice preview alone provides no certified load capacity.

title: Selection-aware edits and revision guards
summary: Carry geometry references and design intent into an edit without guessing which entity you meant.
content_html:
“Make this hole larger” is a clear instruction when two engineers are looking at the same feature. It becomes less clear when the model changes, the selection is lost or a face number is reused. A useful conversational CAD workflow must preserve what was selected, which model revision it belonged to and which requirements should survive the edit.

Selection provides geometric context

Intact lets a user select parts, faces or edges in the viewer, attach references or sketches and describe a question or edit. Before work starts, Ask AI saves the description, native selection, source revision and artifact, references and an optional viewport image. This creates a concrete request that can be read again instead of relying only on a transient highlight.

A practical request might be: “Increase the selected mounting hole to 8 mm. Preserve the other holes and the outside dimensions. Ask before reducing the required clearance.” The selection identifies the intended target; the text states the change and the invariants. A reference image can explain intent, but it should not silently override measurable native geometry.

Understand where Ask AI actually runs

When a supported ChatGPT host exposes the component messaging bridge, Intact can send a follow-up carrying the saved request identity and description. That capability is detected at runtime. It is conditional, rather than a guarantee that every browser or desktop host can insert a request into the current conversation.

In the localhost viewer, Ask AI otherwise starts a separate model-scoped task through the signed-in OpenAI local client automatically. Its progress, answer and clarification replies appear in Intact. That task does not join or impersonate the currently open ChatGPT conversation. The workflow does not require a separate model-service API key.

The Ask AI handoff documentation describes these paths. If a bridge attempt fails, the error remains retryable rather than silently starting a duplicate local task. The release tests distinguish mocked bridge behavior from real local-client execution; live current-chat delivery in Windows ChatGPT was not verified in the 0.16 release report.

Revision guards protect the intended starting point

An edit request belongs to a model state. If another operation changes that state before an edit is applied, the original selection may no longer mean the same thing. Revision guards make that dependency explicit. The task should read the current model, compare the expected revision and reconcile changed context before applying a mutation.

This matters even for simple parts. Adding a fillet can split an edge or replace a face. A numeric face identifier that once described the mounting surface can become stale after rebuilding. Treating the old number as a permanent semantic name would hide ambiguity instead of solving it.

Bind references, then verify them

Intact supports stable labeled references to inspected entities. Same-artifact references retain identity; other matches use geometric signatures, while hole anchors can follow a named feature and center index. These mechanisms have limits. Reordering hole centers changes the index convention, and multiple geometric candidates must not be resolved by guessing.

When a referenced feature disappears, unrelated source changes invalidate its interpretation or several candidates match, reselect and bind the intended entity. Replies preserve conversation context and current references, while stale numeric references are dropped after geometry changes. Explicit ambiguity is a useful result: it tells the user what decision remains unresolved.

Preserve editable intent and check the outcome

For structured projects, the task should retain supported sketches, parameters and feature relationships. Updating an operation should preserve unrelated steps. A staged feature graph is not yet rebuilt geometry, and a failed rebuild should preserve the last valid geometry. Imported STEP and arbitrary Python programs do not automatically become complete parametric feature histories.

After an edit, inspect the resulting native geometry and verify the actual export against the updated requirements. Ask whether the selected hole has the requested diameter, whether other parts remain and whether clearance still passes. A confident answer in the conversation is not a substitute for those checks.

Give questions and analysis the right scope

A read-only question should not mutate CAD. Historical previews remain read-only, and simulation requests cannot change the model. Mechanical Ask AI can run an actual analysis once material, supports and loads are sufficient; missing physical inputs should lead to clarification. Preparation without solver evidence is not a successful engineering result.

See the structured modeling contracts for reference and verification limits. The website demo presents prebuilt browser interactions; real AI and CAD tasks run through the native Windows local setup. Read the system architecture before starting an editing session.

title: What a geometry audit proves—and what it leaves to engineering
summary: Follow a flange through topology checks, native export inspection and design requirements. Learn to read passed, failed and unverified evidence.
content_html:
A geometry audit answers a narrower question than “Is this design ready?” It can show that a solid is valid, a mesh is closed or an exported file preserved the intended components. Those checks matter, but they are different from proving that the design meets its brief or survives its operating conditions. Intact keeps these claims separate so the evidence remains useful.

Begin with measurable intent

Consider an 80 mm diameter flange, 8 mm thick, with a 24 mm bore and six 6 mm through holes on a 60 mm bolt circle. The brief defines more than an envelope: bore concentricity, hole centers, diameter, count and depth all matter. A model could have the correct outside dimensions and still contain blind holes, the wrong bolt circle or a shifted bore.

Ask ChatGPT to save supported requirements before building. State which dimensions are exact, what tolerance applies and which interfaces are critical. Without acceptance criteria, the system can inspect geometry but cannot claim the intended design was verified.

First gate: the object itself

For native solids, Intact checks B-rep validity, finite positive volumes, dimensions and tessellation. For a sampled mesh, it checks finite coordinates, watertightness, winding and positive volume. A mesh check does not turn the mesh into an exact CAD solid.

Bounded healing can address certain kernel or orientation problems only while preserving strict geometric invariants. A repair that changes the required dimensions or discards a feature is a design change, not a harmless correction. A rejected build preserves the last saved revision.

Second gate: the delivered files

The viewport is a tessellated representation. The file a downstream tool receives must be inspected independently. Native STEP reopening checks part identity, dimensions and volume. Other export checks inspect GLB structure and 3MF integrity. This catches cases where a reasonable-looking preview conceals a missing component or an export discrepancy.

Third gate: the requirements

Design verification measures supported saved requirements against actual native geometry. Ask for the measured values and the criterion for each result, not just an overall label. A check may pass, fail or remain unverified. Known failed requirements block the proposal. Missing or unsupported criteria do not become passes.

Sampled thickness or clearance evidence has a bounded scope. A few safe wall-thickness samples do not establish the global minimum across an arbitrary surface. Likewise, a component count does not prove all those components have the correct geometry.

Validation reaches beyond the geometry

Does the model represent the real bracket, manufacturing process and load path? Are the material and supports appropriate? A CAD audit alone cannot answer these questions. Validation needs suitable design references, physical assumptions and, where appropriate, independent analysis or experiments.

For numerical studies, inspect mesh quality, residuals, force or heat balance, refinement and regime limits. A simulation image is not sufficient evidence. An unrefined result stays unverified even if its colors look smooth.

A prompt that asks for evidence

Audit the current flange and verify the saved requirements against the native exported geometry. Report the actual envelope, bore, hole diameters, centers and through depth. Separate passed, failed and unverified checks. Preserve the revision and do not weaken the acceptance criteria.

Use Review and the user tutorial to inspect the result. See the architecture explanation for the complete gate and repair loop.

title: From a ChatGPT brief to a local CAD model
summary: Trace the conversation, MCP tools, isolated Python worker, native kernel and viewer through one controlled modeling request.
content_html:
When you ask Intact for a part, several distinct systems participate. ChatGPT interprets your request. The plugin exposes engineering tools. A CAD engine constructs geometry. A local viewer displays the exported representation. Understanding those responsibilities makes it easier to write a useful brief and diagnose a surprising result.

The conversation defines the task

Begin with purpose, units, dimensions, interfaces and the deliverable. For an enclosure, specify outside size, wall thickness, lid arrangement and mounting features. Call out dimensions that can be assumed and dimensions that must be clarified. Ask for separate named components where you need separate parts.

ChatGPT uses the installed plugin’s workflow instructions and tool descriptions to choose operations. The assistant’s explanation is not a substitute for a measured result. Ask it to retain checkable requirements and report what was actually verified.

MCP connects intent to operations

The Model Context Protocol interface exposes typed engineering operations. Requests include settings and, for existing designs, the current model and revision. Input checks and revision guards help prevent a change based on stale geometry from overwriting a newer design.

For native CAD, a bounded Python program uses build123d and OpenCASCADE. For explicit sketch relationships, the structured route uses FreeCAD constraints and supported feature operations. Sampled TPMS geometry follows a mesh path. The representation determines which measurements and exports are meaningful.

Generated Python runs behind a boundary

The supported runtime uses Linux namespaces and bubblewrap, with filesystem/network isolation and resource limits. Program policy checks supplement this operating-system boundary. CAD generation is disabled when required isolation is unavailable; installation problems should be repaired without bypassing it.

The worker builds a candidate, inspects its geometry and generates artifacts. Audits and saved design requirements are evaluated before publishing an accepted revision. If the build fails, the last accepted design remains available. Source repair should address the failing feature, not change the brief merely to make a check pass.

The viewer closes the loop

Orbit, section and inspect the result. Select a current part, face or edge and ask a specific question or edit. The selected reference carries source identity so the system can detect staleness instead of guessing which later face has the same number.

A small follow-up can be precise: “Move this mounting boss 3 mm in +X. Preserve the bore diameter and the other bosses. Verify the resulting center positions.” For an uncertain idea, request a parameter preview before saving it.

Where your account and computation fit

Your own ChatGPT account provides the AI conversation; the installed local runtime performs CAD and supported numerical work. The current package is a personal plugin installation, not an automatic download triggered by opening ChatGPT. No separate model-service API key is required for the supported signed-in workflow, while account availability and usage limits still apply.

Projects remain local, but selected requests and relevant model context pass to the AI provider through the client. Review the data-flow explanation before using confidential material.

title: Compare design alternatives before changing the accepted model
summary: Use scratch previews, named configurations and read-only Review requests to compare changes with dimensions and evidence.
content_html:
An alternative is easier to judge when its tradeoffs are explicit. “Make this stronger” could mean thicker walls, a rib, a different material or a changed load path. Those choices have different effects on mass, clearance, manufacturing and appearance. A good comparison begins with the question that matters.

Set a baseline

Open the accepted revision and record the relevant envelope, component placement and measured volume. Note which requirements must remain fixed. For an enclosure, the outside footprint, connector positions and mounting pattern may be non-negotiable even while wall thickness changes.

Volume is a geometric measurement. It becomes a mass estimate only with an appropriate density and material assignment. A larger volume is not, by itself, proof of greater stiffness or strength.

Ask Review for options

Press R to open Review. The panel shows the current revision’s measured context and audit status, and can submit read-only AI requests for accuracy checks, alternatives or realistic detail priorities. A useful request is: “Propose three ways to improve this mounting feature. Compare space, likely manufacturing implications and what evidence is still needed. Do not edit the model.”

Keep suggestions separate from completed engineering work. An AI proposal has not been built, checked or analyzed simply because it sounds plausible.

Preview numeric changes

For an existing parameter, ask for a scratch rebuild: “Preview wall thicknesses of 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0 mm. Keep the external envelope fixed. Compare measured volume and internal clearance without changing the saved revision.” Parameter previews perform a noncommitting build and return actual geometry facts.

Some dimensions may not be independently editable. A thicker wall could close a slot or violate a clearance. A failed preview is useful evidence that a dependency needs attention. Do not silently suppress that feature to obtain a successful comparison.

Save named configurations

When a numeric parameter set is worth retaining, ask for a named configuration. Configurations store parameter values, not a general promise that the design is valid under every combination. Applying one rebuilds against the current revision, and the resulting geometry still needs the relevant audit and requirement checks.

Use explicit sketch constraints where relationships must persist. A one-time arithmetic expression in a parameter experiment does not create a permanent dependency between dimensions.

Commit the chosen result and verify it

State which option to apply and which criteria remain unchanged. Ask for measured differences, a snapshot and any failed or unverified checks. Inspect front and side views when changes affect interfaces. Retain the baseline revision for comparison.

If the decision depends on stress, heat flow or motion, use an appropriate study with defined physical inputs. A parameter comparison cannot establish performance that was never computed. Kinematic playback cannot establish contact forces or stability.

Bring the comparison to a design review

Request a pinned-revision presentation with actual views, dimensions, audit context, a component register and factual notes. Label proposed improvements and unverified assumptions clearly. The deck should help the team decide what to test next.

See the practical tool tutorial and the verification chain.

title: Read a simulation result beyond the color plot
summary: Check the physical setup, native boundaries, mesh, residuals, conservation and refinement before interpreting a result.
content_html:
A color plot compresses a large amount of information into an image, but it can also hide an incorrect setup. Before interpreting displacement, stress or temperature, establish what problem was solved and which evidence supports the answer. Intact associates a report with its source geometry and preserves the numerical audit context.

Start with the physical question

Specify the analyzed solid, units, material properties and boundary conditions. For structural work, identify supports and whether a load is a total force, pressure or other supported condition. For steady conduction, specify conductivity and actual thermal boundaries. A wrong boundary selection can produce a numerically tidy answer to the wrong question.

Use native face references and inspect the selected regions. If geometry changes, confirm that the study still refers to the current artifact. Do not assume a face number identifies the same surface after a rebuild.

Check the supported regime

Intact’s bounded mechanical workflows include small-strain linear elasticity, steady thermal conduction and creeping-flow Stokes. They do not establish whole-assembly contact, nonlinear mechanics, turbulence, inertial CFD or multiphysics. Whole-vehicle suspension behavior requires capabilities and inputs beyond a single-solid compression case.

Virtual Analysis is a different tool: it previews prescribed kinematics. Wheel rotation and a moving chassis do not prove traction, collision handling, suspension forces or balance.

Read the effective mesh

Record element counts, quality and actual resolution. Automatic sizing may coarsen an overly fine request to stay within computational limits. The requested element size is not necessarily the size that was solved. A mesh picture helps inspect distribution, but it does not establish convergence.

Refinement compares quantities across successive resolutions. Displacement can stabilize before local stress does. An analysis that stops at a resource budget without meeting the target remains unverified; do not relabel it converged because the final image appears smooth.

Read numerical diagnostics in context

Residuals measure how well the discrete equations were solved. Conservation checks test balances such as applied force versus reaction, or heat input versus heat output. Both are useful, but neither proves that the material values, supports or model dimensions describe the real system.

The headless result audit checks finite fields, residuals, conservation, refinement and supported regime information. Invalid numerical output is rejected. Missing refinement or out-of-regime results remain explicitly unverified or require review.

Use an independent comparison

For a uniform compression block, compare displacement with FL/(EA), stress with F/A and the summed reaction with the total applied force. The 1000 N benchmark works through this example. Agreement on that case provides bounded verification evidence; it is not a certification of arbitrary geometries.

For more complex work, select appropriate reference solutions, experimental data or independent engineering analysis. Document what remains uncertain.

Keep reporting faithful to the result

Read the deformation scale before judging shape changes. Visual amplification is not the physical displacement and does not modify the CAD. Retain units, material values, source revision, mesh information and verification status in exported results and review decks.

Report the study assumptions, effective mesh, peak quantities with units, support reaction or conservation evidence, residual, refinement status and unsupported aspects. Keep failed and unverified checks visible.

Follow the simulation tutorial before preparing your first study.
